# 3. Research Question

Among participants who considered themselves attractive (eg. self-rated attractiveness rating > 6), what is the true population proportion of those who are also rated highly on attractiveness, and is it significantly different from a hypothesized value ( 0.50)?

# 4. Data Description

## 4.1 Data Collection
The researchers recruited graduate and professional students from Columbia University. They reached out to them through mass emails and campus flyers. The experiments were conducted over a span of 2002 to 2004 inclusive. They were done inside a private room at a restaurants and a bar near the university campus. They attended individual events called "waves". During a wave, every participant had a 4-minute "speed date" with every person of the opposite sex in the session. They filled out a confidential scorecard after the short conversation. They indicated whether they would like to meet that person again and rated their partner on six ket attributes.

## 4.2 Key Variables
`attractive_o`: Rating by partner (about the person in the row) at night of event on attractiveness  
`attractive`: Self-rated attractiveness  

## 4.3 Data Structure and Sample Size
Single Row Representation: One row of the data set would represents an individual speed-dating interaction in the speed-dating experiment

Population Representation: We can assume that this sample student represents the larger population of Columbia University students through the past 20 years. This is because the researchers recruited students randomly via mass emails and campus flyers. 

Sample Size: The sample size is 700, consisting of 700 rows from wave 9 which was a single session. The sample size is relatively small but the people from each wave are pulled from the larger population of students from Columbia. This makes it reasonable to provide a stable basis for hypothesis testing.

```{r}
data = read.csv("speeddating.csv")

data$attractive <- as.numeric(as.character(data$attractive))
data$attractive_o <- as.numeric(as.character(data$attractive_o))

nrow(data %>% filter(wave ==9) %>% filter(attractive > 6))
```

```{r}
glimpse(data |> select(attractive, attractive_o))
```


# 5. Graph Description
We will create a sampling distribution graph. We will draw a vertical line on the p-value to compare it with $\alpha$.

- Y-axis: Probability density
- X-axis: Proportion of people that are attractive

# 6. Inference Method
Single population proportion ($p$)

## Steps
- Compute the observed mean proportion in the sample (Point Estimate).
- Calculate the test statistic.
- Standardize the test statistic.
- Compute the p-value under the null hypothesis ($H_0: p = 0.50$).
- Compare the p-value with $\alpha$.

## Interpretation
- Reject $H_0$: If $p < 0.05$, there is a significant difference between the self-perceived and externally-perceived attractiveness.
- Fail to Reject $H_0$: If $p \ge 0.05$, conclude no significant difference exists between the self-perceived and externally-perceived attractiveness.
